newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey may drop customs deal if spurned by EU.
newsitem.headline: Turkey may drop customs deal if spurned by EU.

text.p: Turkey's envoy to the European Union said on Wednesday that Ankara could opt out of a customs union deal with the bloc if it refused to include the Moslem country in its expansion plans, the Anatolian news agency said.
"Our relations with the EU could not survive under these circumstances and customs union could not be continued," envoy Uluc Ozulker told the state-run agency from Strasbourg.
Turkey entered into a customs union with the EU at the start of last year. Ankara saw the deal as a step to full membership.
But in Brussels last Tuesday, the leaders of Christian Democratic and centrist parties from Germany, Belgium, Italy, Luxembourg, Ireland and Spain rejected Turkey's EU candidacy.
The leader of the European People's Party, former Belgian prime minister Wilfried Martens, said Turkey was not a candidate for membership "short-term or long."

Ozulker said Turkey would feel spurned if the group took a decision to exclude it from its expansion plans. Customs union would lose its meaning and its aims, he said, adding that instead of pleading with the EU, Turkey could turn elsewhere.

He did not specify where Turkey would turn, but Turkish secularists and some western countries fear that the country -- 99 percent Moslem but secular -- could turn to its Islamist Middle Eastern neighbours.
Turkey has been governed by an Islamist-led coalition since June and Necmettin Erbakan is the country's first Islamist prime minister in nearly 74 years as a secular republic.
Ozulker told Anatolian the centrist parties' views appeared to betray a Crusader mentality that saw civilisation as the premise of Christians only.
He said Turkey only failed to meet the EU criteria on human rights grounds -- an area in which it has drawn a great deal of Western criticisim.

"Apart from (human rights) Turkey is unmistakably European. The human rights problem is a problem that can be overcome," he said, adding that Turkey was closer to meeting EU criteria than the 11 countries in talks with the EU over joining.
The European Parliament has blocked million of dollars of aid to Turkey, partly as a result of its human rights record.

Turkey's parliament passed the law reforming custody procedures last week but the rights group Amnesty International said it did not go far enough as the law still allowed up to four days of incommunicado detention.
Earlier on Tuesday, Turkey announced the new law and other proposals which it said would focus on preventing torture in police custody and improve efforts to trace people who have disappeared.
